title: LSDE 2.7: 183 audio tags for AI voice lines, a personal tag dictionary, and a shuffle to find a new tak
author: djmisterjon
selftext:
I make LSDE, a desktop editor for game dialogue, localization and narrative scenes. Version 2.7 is mostly about AI voice lines (ElevenLabs) and the keys behind them.

**What changed**

* The audio tag catalog grows to 183: stronger emotions, speech tics, voice timbres, accents and a group of sound effects. A right-click in the text, outside a tag, inserts one before or after the word under the cursor.
* A personal dictionary lets you add your own tags, with a description, and mark favourites that follow you across all your projects.
* A right-click on "Improve for TTS" shuffles the tags of a line, at random or within the same mood, or goes back to the key text.
* Each line keeps its past texts, generated or not, and brings back your draft in progress when you return to it.
* In lip sync, a right-click on the play button plays the take again from the start, and the button shows pause while playing.
* Each AI provider remembers its active key. With rotation ticked, a refused key hands over to the next one, including for ElevenLabs voices.
* An agent can fill the empty file paths of a namespace through the MCP bridge, without touching keys or texts.
* Warnings now show in yellow, and red is kept for errors.

**Why**

Audio tags are how you direct a generated line (a whisper, a sigh, an accent), and a catalog you cannot extend is a ceiling. The dictionary removes it, and the shuffle gives you a quick way to hear other readings of the same line.

How do you direct AI voice lines in your project? Tags in the script, settings per line, or a processing pass afterwards?

replies.author: djmisterjon
replies.body:
hi, yes sry, It depends on demand. My DRM is tied to CPU-specific compilation, which is straightforward to support on widely used Windows x64 systems.

Mac is more complicated, with Apple switching architectures, including the move to Apple Silicon (ARM) in 2020. Testing every configuration would require a fleet of Macs. GitHub Actions’ macOS runners can’t help with code signing or some of the other technical issues I’ve encountered.

Mac support may come eventually, depending on demand. For now, I’m focusing on Windows. Without my DRM, it would already be available.

Linux is also a possibility, especially with the growing migration to the platform, but I’ll wait and see if there’s enough demand.
